title: Water-fed poles and ground-based operations
audience: Trainees and workers on the window cleaning (all heights) and solar panel cleaning tracks, working under supervision. Shared lesson: stored once and referenced by both course manifests. Not an authority to use a pole near overhead lines or from any unstable footing.
learningOutcomes: Explain why ground-based methods are the first option in the height hierarchy and where they still carry hazards.
Inspect a water-fed pole system and identify conditions that stop its use.
Apply overhead-line, wind, public-exclusion and runoff controls to a simulated ground-based job.

instruction.heading: Why ground-based methods come first
instruction.body: A water-fed pole lets a worker clean windows or panels from the ground, so the worker's feet stay on a stable surface. This is why ground-based methods come first in the height hierarchy. A ground-based method is not risk-free, however. The pole is long, often conductive, and can strike overhead services, people or property. It can also fail at its joints or under wind load. The method reduces the need for height; it does not remove the need for planning, an exclusion zone and a stop-work rule.

instruction.heading: Inspect the equipment before use
instruction.body: Before each job, inspect every pole section, joint, seal, hose, filter and nozzle. Look for cracks, dents, bent sections, worn or missing seals, damaged threads and fittings that do not match. Do not fit attachments that the manufacturer has not approved. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for maximum length, water supply and any detergent. A pole with any defect is removed from service, tagged, and reported.

instruction.heading: Overhead electrical lines
instruction.body: Conductive poles can contact overhead power lines and transfer current to the operator. Before extending a pole, survey the area above and beside the work for overhead lines, service drops and any structure that could carry electricity. In New South Wales, the SafeWork NSW code (May 2026) sets 4.0 m for handling conductive materials such as scaffolding, roofing, guttering and pipes near low-voltage overhead service lines, and 3.0 m for ordinary persons near lines up to 132,000 V; the code does not address water-fed poles, so this course treats a water-fed pole as conductive as a precaution. The rule is firm: if a line is within reach, or you cannot confirm the clearance, stop, keep the pole down, and refer the job to the network operator or a qualified person before continuing.

instruction.heading: Wind, public protection and falling objects
instruction.body: A long pole acts like a sail in wind and can become unstable. Set a wind threshold in the job plan and stop when it is exceeded. Keep the public and property out of the drop zone beneath the work area using barriers or a supervisor, and do not allow anyone to walk under a working pole. Plant the base on firm, level ground. If the footing shifts or the pole sways beyond control, lower it and reassess.

instruction.heading: Runoff and chemicals
instruction.body: Wash water, detergent and any approved cleaning product must not run into stormwater. Use only products with a safety data sheet available on site. Choose the lowest-impact method the job allows and collect or divert runoff where the job plan requires it.

instruction.heading: Limits of the method
instruction.body:
A pole does not make an unsafe surface safe. If the surface can only be reached by climbing, leaning out or working from an unstable platform, the ground-based method does not apply and the job returns to the access decision in the scope lesson. Never extend a pole to the point where you are using it to climb, to pull yourself up, or to reach beyond a safe footing. Record each limit you reached and what you did instead.

Licence notice: This lesson does not grant any licence or authority to work at height, near overhead lines or with pressurised equipment.

procedure: Survey the work area for overhead lines, service drops, people, property and footing before the pole is assembled.
Inspect each pole section, joint, seal, hose, filter and nozzle, and remove any defective part from service.
Confirm that every fitting is compatible and approved by the manufacturer.
Set the wind threshold and the exclusion zone in the job plan before starting.
Plant the base on firm, level ground and keep the pole clear of overhead lines at all times.
Use the approved product only, with its safety data sheet on site, and keep runoff out of stormwater.
Stop and lower the pole if the wind, footing, a line or a person enters the zone changes the conditions.
Record the equipment checks, the conditions, any limit reached and the decision taken.

workedExamples.situation: A water-fed pole is needed to clean the first-floor windows of a terrace house. A single overhead service line runs along the front boundary, close to the top of the planned pole reach.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the job proceed with the pole, and what is the first action?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not start. The overhead line is within the possible reach of the pole. In New South Wales the 4.0 m figure is not stated for water-fed poles, so the course applies it as a precaution, and a line within that distance is not approached. Keep the pole down, record the line and its position, and refer to the network operator or a qualified person. The job may resume only if the clearance is confirmed or the job is re-planned to keep the pole and any part of it away from the line.

workedExamples.situation: A worker is using a pole on a ground-level window with a gusty forecast. The pole has a small crack near one joint that was noticed during setup.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must the worker do with the pole?
workedExamples.reasoning: Remove the pole from service. A cracked joint can fail under load, and the crack is a defect that the worker cannot approve for use. Tag the section, record the defect, report it to the supervisor, and use a replacement section only if the manufacturer approves the fit. The wind threshold in the job plan also needs review before any work resumes.

equipmentAndPpe: Water-fed pole sections with manufacturer-approved fittings and a joint inspection checklist
Water supply, filter and approved nozzle as specified by the manufacturer
Approved cleaning product with a safety data sheet kept on site
Barriers or cones for the exclusion zone and a supervisor to hold the zone
Eye protection, gloves and non-slip footwear as specified in the job pack

commonErrors.error: Extending the pole without a check for overhead lines.
commonErrors.prevention: Survey the full reach before assembly and keep the pole down if any line is within reach or unclear.

commonErrors.error: Using a cracked or bent section because it still appears to work.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove any defective section from service, tag it and report it.

commonErrors.error: Letting runoff flow to stormwater through a drain or gutter.
commonErrors.prevention: Divert or collect runoff as the job plan requires and check the state and council rules.

commonErrors.error: Working a long pole in gusty wind.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a wind threshold in the job plan and stop when it is exceeded.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Electrical contact with overhead lines when using conductive poles is a serious hazard. In New South Wales, the SafeWork NSW code (May 2026) sets 4.0 m for conductive materials near low-voltage overhead service lines and 3.0 m for ordinary persons near lines up to 132,000 V.
Chemicals and runoff: stormwater and wastewater rules are state-based.
Licence notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to work at height or near overhead lines.

qualityStandard: Every pole section is inspected and every defect is removed from service before use.
Overhead line checks are recorded, and the job stops where clearance is unconfirmed.
The wind threshold, exclusion zone and runoff control are written in the job plan.
The approved product and its safety data sheet are on site.
documentationEvidence: Equipment inspection record with defects found and action taken
Overhead line survey with positions and the decision on clearance
Wind threshold, exclusion zone and runoff control in the job plan
Product name and safety data sheet reference used on the job
summary: Ground-based methods come first, but a pole can still strike overhead lines, people or property.
Inspect the pole and its fittings before each use and remove defective parts from service.
Stop when a line, the wind, the footing or a person changes the conditions.
Keep runoff out of stormwater and use only approved products with safety data sheets.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a ground-based method come first in the height hierarchy?
options: It keeps the worker's feet on a stable surface and reduces the need for height
It removes all risk from the job and the job plan is then not needed at all
It means no job plan is needed and no risk check is needed for the job
It allows the worker to climb the pole to reach the upper windows quickly

knowledgeChecks.question: A pole section has a crack at a joint. What must happen?
options: Use it carefully on low wind days only
Remove it from service, tag it and report it
Tape the joint and continue to the end of the job
Use it only on the ground floor today

knowledgeChecks.question: An overhead service line is within the possible reach of the pole and its clearance is unconfirmed. What is the correct action?
options: Work quickly before the line is touched and keep the pole raised above it
Ask the customer to turn off the power and continue while you are on the roof
Keep the pole down and refer to the network operator or a qualified person
Use a longer pole for more reach and keep the line in view at all times

knowledgeChecks.question: Which control best protects the public beneath a working pole?
options: A verbal warning to passers-by and a friendly wave
A sign on the house and a note on the gate
Working only at night and only on weekends
An exclusion zone held by barriers or a supervisor

knowledgeChecks.question: What must happen to wash water and detergent during a ground-based clean?
options: They must be kept out of stormwater, as the job plan requires
They may run into stormwater if the volume is small
They may be poured onto the lawn in any amount after the job
They are not relevant to ground-based work and they need no record
